But slow down long enough, and the first words Jesus speaks after the resurrection are not what anyone expected.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c092cd5c80cc7ef09d9860", "tabs": [ "69ceb10ad5f08e5f266cd156", "69c09dca3cac7986ad2990b4", "69c09000d8c5e5cbe7c9eca5", "69c49e25e41167250ba62e6f", "69ceb106e494594cb3ad487d" ], "main-content": "

Easter morning in San Francisco is clear today. Sixty-nine degrees, which means the city is already awake and moving. I am too. And I am catching myself doing what I do every year: rushing past the details of a story I think I already know.

The problem with knowing the ending is that you stop hearing the story. The resurrection of Jesus is among the most familiar events in Western history. We know he rises. We know the tomb is empty. We know the disciples are confused and then overjoyed. So we nod along. We pass the familiar words without pausing. But the details of Easter morning, if you let them slow you down, are not what you expect.

The women arrive first. Mary Magdalene is there, weeping outside the tomb. The disciples have come and gone — Peter and John running, looking, not yet understanding, returning to their homes. Mary stays. She is alone at the tomb when Jesus speaks to her.

N.T. Wright makes a point worth stopping on: if someone in the first century had wanted to invent a fictional story about people seeing Jesus, they would never have cast a woman in the starring role. Not in that culture. A woman's testimony carried no legal weight. If you were building a persuasive case, you would have chosen differently. The fact that Mary is there, named, first — that detail is not a literary device. It is the mark of something recorded as it happened.

Then comes the first thing the risen Jesus says. Not to the disciples. To Mary. And it is not what you expect. No triumph. No \"I told you so.\" No declaration of invincibility or ultimate authority.

He says: \"Go and tell my brothers: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.\"

My Father and your Father. My God and your God.

That is the shift. Not a servant-master relationship surviving death, but something new. Something he had named the night before he was arrested: \"I no longer call you servants. I call you friends.\" (John 15:15) The resurrection is not only the end of death. It is the beginning of a different kind of belonging. Wright describes it as a new world springing to life — not a reward distributed to followers, but a relationship extended to brothers. Jesus could have said anything. He said that.

If you know the Easter story well, I want to ask you to do something harder than reading it. Let it surprise you again. Read slowly past the part you think you know and look for the place where the story does something you didn't expect.

The first words Jesus speaks after the resurrection are not about what he proved. They are about what he wants you to know: that Yahweh is his Father and yours. Not a ruler to be managed from a distance. Not a principle to be applied. A relationship extended to you, in person, on Easter morning.

He rose. And the first thing he did was not declare victory. He used his Father's name like it was also yours.

Perhaps it always was.
